items.explanation: The Proclamation Line along the Appalachians barred colonial settlement westward to stabilize the frontier cheaply after Pontiac's uprising. Colonists who had fought in the French and Indian War — and speculators holding western land claims — saw this as London sacrificing their interests, feeding the grievances that would fuel the imperial crisis.
options: (A) A royal grant of western lands to French settlers as compensation for their wartime losses.
(B) A mass return migration of colonists to Britain in search of affordable farmland.
(C) The complete end of all trade between British colonists and American Indian nations.
(D) Resentment among land-hungry colonists and speculators who believed their wartime sacrifices had earned them access to western lands.
items.stem: The most immediate consequence of the Proclamation of 1763 for British colonists was which of the following?
items.stimulus: "And We do further declare it to be Our Royal Will and Pleasure... to reserve under our Sovereignty, Protection, and Dominion, for the use of the said Indians... all the Lands and Territories lying to the Westward of the Sources of the Rivers which fall into the Sea from the West and North West... And We do hereby strictly forbid, on Pain of our Displeasure, all our loving Subjects from making any Purchases or Settlements whatever... of the Lands above reserved, without our especial leave and Licence for that Purpose first obtained." — Royal Proclamation of 1763

option_explanations.A: This never happened. Britain did not grant western lands to French settlers after the war — France had been defeated and lost Canada and Louisiana east of the Mississippi entirely. The Proclamation reserved the western territory for Native nations and closed it to all settlement, not reassigned it to the French.
option_explanations.B: The opposite of the colonial reaction. Rather than sailing back to Britain, land-hungry colonists kept pushing west across the Proclamation Line — Daniel Boone's pathfinding and squatter settlements of the late 1760s show the pressure ran toward the frontier, not back across the Atlantic.
option_explanations.C: The Proclamation restricted where colonists could settle and buy land, but it did not end trade with Native nations — Britain actually continued to manage and license the Indian trade. A 'complete end of all trade' misreads a settlement ban as a trade embargo.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Proclamation Line ran along the Appalachians and forbade settlement west of it. To colonists who had fought and died in the French and Indian War — and to speculators holding western land claims from colonial charters — this felt like London confiscating the war's prize to save the cost of frontier defense. That sense of sacrificed interests was the immediate consequence, and it became one of the early grievances of the imperial crisis.

items.explanation: Colonists who had fought in the French and Indian War expected the trans-Appalachian west as a reward; the ban on settlement instead signaled that imperial interests (avoiding war, managing the new empire) outranked colonial ones — an early grievance feeding revolutionary sentiment.
options: (A) It united British colonists and Native peoples in shared suspicion of London's imperial motives.
(B) It sharply reduced the flow of British immigrants to North America.
(C) It heightened military tensions between Britain and France in North America.
(D) It angered colonists, who saw it as an unjust restriction imposed by a distant government.
items.stem: The Royal Proclamation of 1763 most directly contributed to which of the following?

option_explanations.A: This reverses the two sides' reactions. Colonists resented the ban because it blocked their access to western land; Native peoples, especially those who had just fought in Pontiac's uprising, welcomed the protection of their territory. There was no shared suspicion uniting them — their interests ran in opposite directions.
option_explanations.B: British immigration to North America continued through the 1760s and 1770s; the Proclamation line regulated settlement location on the frontier, not entry into the colonies. Immigration flows were not its target or its effect.
option_explanations.C: This is off by a decade and a war. The 1763 Treaty of Paris ended the French and Indian War and removed France from mainland North America entirely. There was no ongoing Franco-British military tension in North America for the Proclamation to heighten — that chapter had closed.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The colonists' reading was political, not technical: a distant government in London had drawn a line across territory they believed they had earned by fighting France, barring them from settling it. The anger was not really about the map — it was about who had the right to decide, which made the Proclamation an early lesson in how imperial management could feel like tyranny.

items.explanation: The proclamation was part of a post-1763 imperial reorganization: Britain sought tighter control — regulating western settlement, stationing troops, and extracting revenue through new taxes — to manage a vastly enlarged and debt-ridden empire.
options: (A) Britain's move to give the colonies greater control over their own internal affairs.
(B) Britain's effort to consolidate imperial control over its North American empire.
(C) Britain's attempt to suppress revolutionary ideas already spreading in the colonies.
(D) Britain's shift from mercantilist regulation toward free-market capitalism.
items.stem: The Royal Proclamation of 1763 is best understood in the context of which broader development?

option_explanations.A: This is the exact opposite of the broader development. After 1763 Britain moved to reduce colonial self-direction — tightening customs enforcement, asserting Parliament's right to legislate for the colonies, and reserving decisions about western land to London. Greater colonial control over internal affairs was what colonists demanded, not what London offered.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Proclamation belongs to the post-1763 imperial reorganization: Britain had doubled its North American territory, inherited a massive war debt, and faced Pontiac's uprising. The response was consolidation — regulating western settlement, stationing a standing army in America (and then taxing colonists to pay for it), and extracting revenue through the Sugar, Stamp, and Townshend measures. The Proclamation was the first step in that tightening.
option_explanations.C: A decade too early. In 1763 there was no revolutionary movement to suppress — the imperial crisis began with the Stamp Act in 1765, and independence talk came later still. The Proclamation was aimed at frontier stability and imperial economy, not at silencing colonial radicals who did not yet exist.
option_explanations.D: Britain did not move toward free-market capitalism in 1763; it doubled down on mercantilism. The Navigation Acts stayed in force and enforcement tightened, and the whole revenue program of the 1760s assumed the empire existed for the mother country's economic benefit. Adam Smith would not publish The Wealth of Nations until 1776.

items.explanation: The cartoon shows Britannia dismembered, her severed limbs labeled as colonies, ships idle in the background, an olive branch rejected at her feet, and the motto 'Date Obolum Bellisario' ('give a farthing to Belisarius' — the Roman general reduced to beggary). Franklin warns Parliament that taxation will kill the empire's prosperity, not save it.
options: (A) The thirteen colonies should unite to press their grievances more forcefully against Britain.
(B) The colonists needed stronger militias to defend themselves against British attack after 1763.
(C) British tax policies risked crippling — even dismembering — the British Empire itself.
(D) A British standing army in America would inevitably destroy colonial liberties.
items.stem: [Image description: a 1767 political cartoon by Benjamin Franklin, 'Magna Britannia: Her Colonies Reduc'd.' A dismembered female figure of Britannia lies fallen from a globe, her severed limbs labeled with the names of North American colonies; British merchant ships sit idle in the background; a rejected olive branch lies on the ground; a banner across her body reads 'Date Obolum Bellisario' — 'give a farthing to Belisarius,' the Roman general reduced to begging.] What is the cartoon's central warning?

option_explanations.A: The cartoon's plea runs toward London, not toward the colonies. Franklin is not urging the colonies to organize harder against Britain; he is warning Britain about what its own policies are doing to the empire. Colonial unity (his earlier 'Join, or Die' theme) is not this cartoon's subject.
option_explanations.B: Militias appear nowhere in the cartoon's imagery or message. It shows a dismembered Britannia, idle merchant ships, and a rejected olive branch — all symbols of lost commerce and rejected reconciliation, not of military self-defense. The subject is economic policy, not armed resistance.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Britannia lies dismembered, her severed limbs labeled as the colonies — Franklin's visual argument that taxation is literally tearing the empire apart. The idle merchant ships show the commerce Britain is sacrificing, and the rejected olive branch warns that conciliation is being thrown away. The 'Date Obolum Bellisario' motto drives it home: persist in this taxation, and the empire will be reduced to beggary like the fallen Roman general Belisarius.
option_explanations.D: The cartoon is not about a standing army. No soldiers or armies appear in the imagery, and the policy under attack is taxation — the Stamp Act crisis of 1765–66. Fears about standing armies were real in colonial rhetoric, but they belong to the post-1768 occupation of Boston, not to this cartoon's warning.

items.explanation: Franklin lived in London in the 1760s–70s and lobbied Parliament directly against the Stamp Act. The cartoon's plea — repeal taxes before the empire is torn apart — was aimed at the MPs who could repeal them.
options: (A) Members of Parliament, whom Franklin lobbied to repeal the Stamp Act.
(B) Boston merchants organizing nonimportation boycotts.
(C) Pennsylvania backcountry settlers on the frontier.
(D) Members of the Sons of Liberty organizing protests against British policy.
items.stem: Franklin most likely intended this cartoon for which audience?

option_explanations.A: Correct. Franklin was living in London through the 1760s and 1770s as a colonial agent, and this cartoon was a lobbying instrument: it warned Members of Parliament that the Stamp Act was destroying the empire's prosperity and begged them to repeal it before reconciliation became impossible. The audience was the people with the power to repeal — Parliament.
option_explanations.B: Boston merchants were already organizing nonimportation against the Stamp Act; they needed no persuasion. A cartoon published in London pleading for repeal was addressed to the repealers, not to colonists who were already boycotting.
option_explanations.C: Frontier settlers had little to do with the Stamp Act fight, which centered on merchants, printers, and lawyers in the port cities. A sophisticated political cartoon circulated in London was not aimed at backcountry farmers.
option_explanations.D: The Sons of Liberty were already organizing protests against British policy — they were the converted, not the audience. Franklin's cartoon spoke to Parliament, the body whose votes he was trying to change, with the empire-as-dismembered-body image as his argument.

items.explanation: The rejected olive branch at Britannia's feet symbolizes discarded reconciliation. The same hope for a peaceful settlement animated the Olive Branch Petition (July 1775), in which the Second Continental Congress affirmed loyalty to George III and pleaded for reconciliation even as fighting had begun.
options: (A) Paul Revere's 1770 engraving of the Boston Massacre, which inflamed anti-British feeling.
(B) The 1768 Treaty of Fort Stanwix, which redrew the boundary with the Iroquois.
(C) The Olive Branch Petition of 1775, professing loyalty while seeking reconciliation.
(D) Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776), which demanded immediate independence.
items.stem: The cartoon's hope that the imperial crisis could still be resolved peacefully was most similarly expressed in which of the following?

option_explanations.A: Revere's engraving did the opposite of expressing hope for peaceful resolution — it depicted the Boston Massacre as a deliberate slaughter to inflame anti-British feeling and mobilize colonial resistance. It is an image of propaganda for confrontation, not of reconciliation.
option_explanations.B: The Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1768) was a land agreement between Britain and the Iroquois that redrew the boundary of Native territory — a frontier diplomacy matter, not a statement about reconciling Britain with its colonies. It expresses nothing about the imperial crisis between London and the colonists.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The rejected olive branch at Britannia's feet is Franklin's symbol of discarded reconciliation, and the same spirit — professing loyalty to George III while pleading for a peaceful settlement even after bloodshed — animated the Olive Branch Petition of July 1775. The Second Continental Congress adopted it after Lexington and Concord, affirming allegiance to the king and asking him to intervene for peace. Like the cartoon, it assumed the break was not yet final.
option_explanations.D: Paine's Common Sense is the anti-Olive-Branch: published in January 1776, it demanded immediate and total independence, attacked monarchy itself, and made reconciliation unthinkable. It represents the moment the cartoon's hope died, not a parallel expression of it.

items.explanation: Washington writes that 'we have probably had too good an opinion of human nature in forming our confederation' and that men will not carry measures 'into execution' without 'a coercive power.' The immediate context is the mid-1780s: unpaid war debts, collapsed commerce, and brewing unrest like Shays's Rebellion, which convinced Washington the Confederation lacked the power to govern.
options: (A) Parliament's passage of the Coercive Acts closing the port of Boston.
(B) Disputes among the states over the terms of the Treaty of Paris.
(C) The outbreak of revolution in France and its threat to American trade.
(D) The Confederation Congress's inability to raise revenue, pay its debts, or suppress domestic unrest.
items.stem: Washington's letter was written most directly in response to which of the following?
items.stimulus: "We have errors to correct. We have probably had too good an opinion of human nature in forming our confederation. Experience has taught us that men will not adopt and carry into execution measures the best calculated for their own good without the intervention of a coercive power. I do not conceive that we can exist long as a nation without having lodged somewhere a power which will pervade the whole Union in as energetic a manner as the authority of the state governments extends over the several states.... What a triumph for the advocates of despotism to find that we are incapable of governing ourselves, and that systems founded on the basis of equal liberty are merely ideal and fallacious." — George Washington to John Jay, August 1, 1786

option_explanations.A: Wrong decade. The Coercive (Intolerable) Acts were passed in 1774, during the imperial crisis — more than a decade before Washington wrote this letter, and before the Confederation even existed. He is writing about the confederation formed after independence, not about Parliament's pre-war punishments.
option_explanations.B: Disputes over the Treaty of Paris were a symptom, not the subject. Washington's letter is about the structural weakness of the Confederation — Congress's lack of coercive power over the states — illustrated by unpaid debts and unenforceable measures generally, not by diplomatic wrangling over the treaty's terms.
option_explanations.C: The French Revolution began in 1789; Washington's letter dates from the mid-1780s, when France was still a monarchy and an American ally. A threat to American trade from revolutionary France belongs to the 1790s, years after this letter.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Washington wrote in the mid-1780s, when the Confederation Congress could not raise revenue because it had no power to tax, could not compel states to honor requisitions, could not pay the war debt or the army's back pay, and could not reliably suppress domestic unrest — Shays's Rebellion (1786–87) was the alarming proof. His phrase 'too good an opinion of human nature' is a confession that the Articles trusted voluntary cooperation and left Congress without 'a coercive power.'

items.explanation: In context, Washington means the Confederation's framers trusted too much in voluntary compliance: states ignored requisitions, Congress couldn't tax or enforce laws, and 'too good an opinion of human nature' = too much faith that citizens and states would act for the common good without coercion. Shays's Rebellion (1786–87) seemed to confirm it.
options: (A) Deist theology had wrongly discarded the Calvinist doctrine of original sin.
(B) Americans had naively trusted Britain to honor the Treaty of Paris (1783).
(C) The army had misjudged the willingness of Ohio Valley tribes to live peacefully alongside white settlers.
(D) The Articles' framers trusted too much in voluntary cooperation and gave Congress no coercive power.
items.stem: In the context of the letter, Washington's remark that Americans 'had too good an opinion of human nature' most nearly means which of the following?

option_explanations.A: Washington is making a political point, not a theological one. His 'too good an opinion of human nature' is not about Deist theology versus the Calvinist doctrine of original sin — it is about the practical failure of a government that assumed states and citizens would voluntarily do their duty without enforcement.
option_explanations.B: The letter is not about Britain's conduct. Washington's complaint is directed inward, at the American confederation's design — Congress's inability to compel compliance from the states — not at whether Britain was honoring the 1783 treaty.
option_explanations.C: The letter says nothing about the Ohio Valley tribes or the army's relations with them. 'Human nature' here refers to the states and citizens whose voluntary cooperation the Articles relied on, not to Native peoples on the frontier.
option_explanations.D: Correct. In context, Washington is diagnosing the Articles of Confederation: their framers trusted that the states would voluntarily fund Congress, honor requisitions, and carry out national measures — and experience had proved otherwise. 'Too good an opinion of human nature' means too much faith in uncoerced compliance, the flaw that left Congress with no power to tax, regulate, or enforce.

items.explanation: Washington's remedy for a feeble confederation was a stronger national government — the position that carried the Philadelphia Convention and the ratification fight. He became the Constitution's most prestigious supporter and the first president under it.
options: (A) They would have urged the United States to honor the 1778 alliance by joining France's war against Britain in 1793.
(B) They would have opposed chartering the Bank of the United States in 1791.
(C) They would have supported ratification of the Constitution in 1787–1788.
(D) They would have opposed the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798.
items.stem: Americans who shared Washington's outlook in this letter would most likely have taken which of the following later positions?

option_explanations.A: Washington did the opposite. In 1793, when France's war with Britain raised the question of honoring the 1778 alliance, Washington issued the Proclamation of Neutrality, keeping the United States out of the war. Someone sharing his outlook would have backed neutrality, not intervention for France.
option_explanations.B: Washington signed the Bank bill into law in 1791, after Hamilton persuaded him it was constitutional. Supporters of Washington's strong-government outlook backed the Bank of the United States; opposition to it came from Jefferson and Madison.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Washington's letter concludes that the Confederation's weakness can only be cured by a government with real, coercive national power — the exact argument for the Constitution. He presided over the Philadelphia Convention, lent his prestige to ratification, and became the first president under the new system. Anyone sharing this letter's outlook would have been a Federalist for ratification in 1787–88.
option_explanations.D: The Alien and Sedition Acts (1798) were supported by the Federalist camp — the political heirs of Washington's strong-national-government outlook — and opposed by Jeffersonian Republicans. Someone sharing Washington's outlook would have backed, not opposed, measures strengthening federal authority.

items.explanation: Hamilton's catalog of 'national humiliation' — unpaid debts, commerce 'at the lowest point of declension,' foreign disrespect — is traced to a Congress that could not tax, regulate commerce, or enforce its resolutions. His remedy was a national government with exactly those powers, the case Federalist No. 15 makes for the Constitution that the Philadelphia Convention was then framing.
options: (A) The rise of Democratic-Republican societies opposing the Washington administration.
(B) The addition of a Bill of Rights to protect individual liberties from federal power.
(C) The drafting of a Constitution creating a stronger national government with powers to tax and regulate commerce.
(D) The issuance of Washington's Proclamation of Neutrality in the war between Britain and France.
items.stem: Hamilton's diagnosis in this passage most directly foreshadowed which of the following developments?
items.stimulus: "We may... be said to have reached almost the last stage of national humiliation. There is scarcely any thing that can wound the pride or degrade the character of an independent nation which we do not experience... Do we owe debts to foreigners and to our citizens...? There remains without any proper or satisfactory provision for their discharge. Is commerce of importance to national wealth? Ours is at the lowest point of declension." — Alexander Hamilton, Federalist No. 15, 1787

option_explanations.A: The Democratic-Republican societies were the opposition to Hamilton's program — grassroots clubs that criticized the Washington administration's policies. Hamilton's diagnosis called for more national power, not for the societies that resisted it; they were his adversaries' instrument, not his remedy's result.
option_explanations.B: The Bill of Rights was demanded by the Anti-Federalists — the opponents of Hamilton's strong national government — as the price of ratification. Hamilton himself argued in Federalist No. 84 that a bill of rights was unnecessary and even dangerous. It was not the development his diagnosis pointed toward.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Hamilton's 'national humiliation' — debts with 'no proper or satisfactory provision for their discharge,' commerce 'at the lowest point of declension,' foreign contempt — is laid at the feet of a Congress that could not tax, could not regulate commerce, and could not enforce its own resolutions. His prescribed remedy, argued across the Federalist essays including No. 15, was a new national government endowed with exactly those powers: the Constitution the Philadelphia Convention was then drafting.
option_explanations.D: Washington's Proclamation of Neutrality (1793) concerned foreign policy toward the Anglo-French war, six years after Federalist No. 15. Hamilton's diagnosis in this passage is about domestic governmental weakness — revenue, commerce, enforcement — not about which European war to avoid.

items.explanation: Britain's refusal to evacuate its Great Lakes forts after 1783 — holding them until the U.S. compensated Loyalists — was, for Hamilton, the concrete humiliation proving the Confederation could not command foreign respect.
options: (A) Britain's refusal to evacuate its Great Lakes forts after the Treaty of Paris (1783).
(B) Spain's military reconquest of Florida from the United States.
(C) French-backed raids by Native allies on New England settlements.
(D) Dutch demands that American merchant ships pay tribute payments in order to dock in Holland.
items.stem: Which of the following specific developments best illustrates the 'national humiliation' Hamilton describes?

option_explanations.A: Correct. After the Treaty of Paris (1783) ended the Revolutionary War, Britain kept its forts in the Great Lakes region — in territory the treaty had ceded to the United States — refusing to evacuate until Americans compensated Loyalists for confiscated property. A Congress that could neither pay nor compel had to tolerate foreign troops on American soil: for Hamilton, the very image of 'national humiliation.' Britain finally evacuated the forts under Jay's Treaty (1794).
option_explanations.B: Spain never reconquered Florida from the United States. Britain returned Florida to Spain in the 1783 Treaty of Paris settlement, and Spain held it peacefully until ceding it to the U.S. in 1819 (Adams-Onís Treaty). There was no Spanish military reconquest of American-held Florida.
option_explanations.C: French-backed Native raids on New England belong to the colonial wars of the 1600s and 1700s — King William's, Queen Anne's, and the French and Indian War — when France was a North American power. After 1763 France was gone from the continent, so this could not be a Confederation-era humiliation.
option_explanations.D: This confuses two different humiliations. In the 1780s–90s it was the Barbary states of North Africa that demanded tribute from American merchant ships, not the Dutch. The Netherlands was an American ally in the Revolution (and the site of John Adams's crucial 1782 loan), not a tribute-demanding power.

items.explanation: Hamilton's Federalist essays were written to win ratification of the Constitution — the stronger national government he believed necessary. He attended the Philadelphia Convention, signed the Constitution, and led the ratification campaign in New York.
options: (A) Abandoning neutrality for an aggressive, interventionist foreign policy.
(B) Replacing the Articles with a stronger central government.
(C) Building military alliances with Native nations against European powers.
(D) Expanding the army while cutting all domestic government spending.
items.stem: To remedy the problems identified in the passage, Hamilton advocated which of the following?

option_explanations.A: Hamilton was a champion of neutrality, not interventionism. As Washington's Treasury secretary he helped shape the Proclamation of Neutrality (1793), keeping the young republic out of Europe's wars. An aggressive, interventionist foreign policy was the opposite of his counsel.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Everything in Hamilton's diagnosis points to the structural fix: the Articles had to be replaced by a stronger central government with the powers the Confederation lacked — taxation, regulation of commerce, enforcement of national law. That was the case he made in the Federalist essays, the Constitution he signed at Philadelphia, and the ratification campaign he led in New York.
option_explanations.C: Hamilton never proposed Native alliances as the remedy for the Confederation's problems. His program was institutional — a new frame of government — not a diplomatic-military scheme with Native nations, with whom the early republic's relations were in fact adversarial.
option_explanations.D: This half-inverts Hamilton's program. He did want a stronger federal establishment — including funding the national debt and a national bank — which meant using federal financial power, not dismantling domestic government. 'Cutting all domestic government spending' contradicts his entire financial system of assumption, funding, and national credit.
